summary: Psalm 75 opens with communal thanks because God's name is near and his works are being told. The poem then shifts into divine speech about an appointed time for judgment, warns arrogant and wicked people not to boast, and ends by contrasting the downfall of the wicked with the lifting up of the righteous.
whyItMatters: Within Psalms, this chapter gives a compact statement of God's judging rule: human status is not finally secured by direction, power, or boasting. It also shows how praise, warning, and judgment imagery can stand together in Israel's prayer book.

context.author: The heading associates the psalm with Asaph; in Psalms, such headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, collection, or performance setting, and their exact historical force is debated.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that received Psalms as public and private prayer.
context.date: Psalm 75 cannot be securely assigned to a single date. It belongs to a Psalter whose poems and collections developed over centuries, from the monarchy through the postexilic period.
context.setting: Book III of Psalms, a section that includes sanctuary, crisis, and questions about God's rule; this psalm speaks in a worship setting shaped by thanksgiving, warning, and confidence in judgment.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, with a musical heading, shifts of speaker, vivid images, and the performance marker Selah.

outline.heading: Thanksgiving near God's name
outline.note: The community gives thanks because God's Name is near and people recount his wondrous works.

outline.heading: God's appointed judgment
outline.note: A first-person voice announces an appointed time for blameless judgment and says he holds firm the pillars of a quaking earth.

outline.heading: Warning to the proud
outline.note: The arrogant and wicked are told not to boast, lift up the horn, or speak with a stiff neck.

outline.heading: Exaltation belongs to God
outline.note: Exaltation does not come from east, west, or south; God is judge, lowering one and lifting another.

outline.heading: The cup for the wicked
outline.note: Yahweh's cup is pictured as foaming, spiced wine that the wicked of the earth must drink to the dregs.

outline.heading: Praise and reversal
outline.note: The speaker promises lasting praise to the God of Jacob and announces that the horns of the wicked will be cut off while the righteous are lifted up.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. To the tune of “Do Not Destroy.” A Psalm by Asaph. A song. We give thanks to you, God. We give thanks, for your Name is near. Men tell about your wondrous works.
keyVerses.why: This opening anchors the psalm in thanksgiving and introduces the nearness of God's name and remembered works.

keyVerses.text: But God is the judge. He puts down one, and lifts up another.
keyVerses.why: This sentence states the chapter's central claim about judgment and reversal.

keyVerses.text: For in Yahweh’s hand there is a cup, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours it out. Indeed the wicked of the earth drink and drink it to its very dregs.
keyVerses.why: The cup image gives the psalm its strongest picture of judgment on the wicked.

keyVerses.text: I will cut off all the horns of the wicked, but the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up.
keyVerses.why: The final verse completes the contrast between wicked and righteous by returning to the image of horns as raised or cut off.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The opening uses a communal voice: “We give thanks to you, God.” Verses 2–3 present God speaking as the judge who chooses the time and holds the earth’s pillars. Verse 9 returns to a singer’s promise of praise, while the final judging voice is not explicitly identified. The changes are carried by the words themselves rather than labels assigning every line to a performer.

questions.question: What does the heading add to the psalm?
questions.answer: The heading gives performance and collection signals: “For the Chief Musician,” a tune name, “A Psalm by Asaph,” and “A song.” These connect the poem with music and the Asaph tradition. They preserve its worship setting without allowing the exact first performance or the melody to be reconstructed.

questions.question: What does it mean that God's Name is near?
questions.answer: Verse 1 says, “your Name is near,” and links that nearness with people telling about God's wondrous works. In Psalms, God's name can stand for God as known, invoked, and praised by the worshiping community. The verse does not describe a location; it presents God's nearness as a reason for thanksgiving.

questions.question: What is the “appointed time”?
questions.answer: Verse 2 says, “When I choose the appointed time, I will judge blamelessly.” The chapter does not identify a calendar date or historical event. Its emphasis is that judgment belongs to the speaker's chosen time, not to the timing demanded by arrogant or wicked people.

questions.question: Why does the earth quake if God is holding its pillars?
questions.answer: Verse 3 pictures “the earth and all its inhabitants” quaking, while the speaker says, “I firmly hold its pillars.” The image holds instability and restraint together: the world trembles, but it is not abandoned. “Selah” marks a pause or performance signal whose exact force is uncertain.

questions.question: What does “horn” mean here?
questions.answer: The chapter uses “horn” as an image of pride, strength, or status. The wicked are told not to lift it up in verses 4-5, and verse 10 says the horns of the wicked will be cut off while the horns of the righteous are lifted up. The image lets the psalm describe boasting and reversal without turning it into a literal body part.

questions.question: Why mention east, west, and south?
questions.answer: Verses 6-7 say that exaltation does not come from east, west, or south, because God is the judge. The point is not geography for its own sake, but the denial that promotion finally comes from human direction or source. The psalm immediately grounds that denial in God's power to put down one and lift up another.

questions.question: What is the cup in Yahweh's hand?
questions.answer: Verse 8 describes a cup in Yahweh’s hand, full of foaming, mixed wine, poured out for the wicked to drink to the dregs. The image makes judgment an overwhelming portion that they must consume completely. Drinking the sediment at the bottom emphasizes that none of the sentence is left behind.

questions.question: How does the ending relate to the opening thanks?
questions.answer: The opening thanks God because his name is near and his works are being told. The closing section returns to praise with “I will declare this forever” and “I will sing praises to the God of Jacob.” The final verse then states the promised reversal: wicked power is cut off and the righteous are lifted up. Praise and judgment remain joined through the ending.

glossary.def: A performance-related title in the heading. It signals that the psalm was associated with musical use, though the exact ancient performance setting is not fully recoverable from the chapter alone.
The tune named in the heading. The words are preserved, but the ancient melody is not.
A Levite associated with musical praise in 1 Chronicles. The heading places this song within the worship tradition bearing his name.
A preserved Hebrew performance marker in verse 3. Its exact instruction is uncertain, so many translations keep the word rather than replacing it.
An image used in this chapter for raised power, pride, or status. The wicked lift it up arrogantly, while the righteous have their horns lifted up at the end.
The image in verse 8 for judgment held and poured out by Yahweh, which the wicked drink to the dregs.
